Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries:

With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. # v0.34.0

**1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new).** Thank you!

## TL;DR

- **10 new models** (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
- **Extensible KV cache is on by default:** vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now **remove `gpu_memory_utilization`** from your configs.
- **Model Runner V1 is gone.** Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
- **Big speedups** on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
- **Upgrade check:** default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and `huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0` is required. See [Before you upgrade](#before-you-upgrade).

## Before you upgrade

> [!IMPORTANT]
> These changes can break existing setups.

| Change | What to do | PR |
|---|---|---|
| Model Runner V1 removed | Remove `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0`; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to `vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor`. | #63373 |
| Default `--block-size` is 64 (was 16) | Pass `-

### Features

* **api:** add Google-managed data controls for Google Cloud projects
* **api:** add Google-managed data controls for user profiles
* **api:** add support for compliance review cases, notices, and items


### Bug Fixes

* **client:** honor proxy and trust_env when proxy variables are set

  `DefaultHttpxClient` and `DefaultAsyncHttpxClient` read `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY` even when the caller passed `proxy=` or `trust_env=False`, and the variables won. Now `proxy=` is used for every request and the variables are not read, and `trust_env=False` ignores them, as in plain `httpx2`.

  What you may notice: with `proxy=` set, a host listed in `NO_PROXY` used to be reached directly and now goes through your proxy. To keep a host off the proxy, pass `mounts={"all://that.host": None}`.


### Chores

* **docs:** drop the provisional naming note from the Google Cloud client README
* **docs:** name both causes of the tool use limit error
* **docs:** update example workspace and API key IDs


### Documentation

* show what enum values mean

<details open>

ggml: allow input async copies (#30685)

* ggml: allow input async copies

Copy the host inputs of a split with set_tensor_async followed by a
single synchronize, instead of one blocking copy per input. This is
opt-in per device through the new async_host_input cap, which only
CUDA sets. Other backends keep the current path.

The async path is used without pipeline parallelism only. With
pipeline parallelism, the input backend also waits on the slot event
before an async copy, since CUDA peer copies run on the source stream.
This replaces the synchronize on graph reuse in process_ubatch.

* remove sched change

* tests : add get_props to test-alloc dummy device

* tests : check that sched inputs can be overwritten after compute_async

* ggml : rename async_host_input to fast_async_host_input, address review comments

</details>

Because these pitfalls are common, if you’ve worked on any AI product, you’ve probably seen them before.

The technical metrics on AI for cybersecurity now indicate that recent advances are enabling attackers more than defenders and that AI is regularly being used in attacks. This is in line with daily news stories on the “vulnpocalypse” and “Black October.” Surprisingly though, data on real-world impacts of cyber attacks tells a less dire story. If this trend continues, it could indicate that attribution and punishment matter at least as much as attackers’ technical capabilities.

The post Judge the Cyber Apocalypse by the Data, Not the Headlines appeared first on Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) chatbots are increasingly used by patients seeking cancer information, but their safety when users present evidence-misaligned beliefs about treatment remains uncharacterized. We hypothesized that LLMs exhibit validation bias, affirming rather than correcting such beliefs, and evaluated this with a 2x2x2 factorial design crossing conversation format (single-turn vs multi-turn), treatment type (evidence-based vs alternative), and query valence (positive vs negative). Framing was evidence-aligned (supporting evidence-based treatments or questioning alternative therapies) or evidence-misaligned (promoting alternative treatments or questioning evidence-based therapies). We analyzed 1,272 conversations (6,360 interactions) across 14 LLMs from 6 vendors, scored by an LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) validated against human annotation on a 6-dimension safety rubric. The primary outcome was the unsafe response rate, defined as a Weak classification or any critical failure. Abstract: Estimating the quality of generative AI workflows is challenging because these workflows comprise multiple stages, and errors can propagate across them, making end-to-end performance depend not only on the accuracy of individual models but also on how their outputs affect downstream stages. Each stage can use one of many candidate models. Estimating end-to-end workflow quality by deploying and evaluating every resulting model configuration is therefore prohibitively expensive. As a result, existing approaches face a tradeoff between estimation cost and accuracy: inexpensive methods often produce unreliable quality estimates, while accurate methods require deploying and evaluating many workflow configurations. In this paper, we introduce DAGGER, a framework for estimating the quality of generative AI workflows without exhaustive deployment and profiling. DAGGER represents a workflow as a graph, in which nodes correspond to stages and edges capture how outputs from one stage affect subsequent stages.
